meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · Materials science · solo · 6 hours
meta.note: 6-hour run. The verifier accepted 1 of 25 credited claims; 1 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Enriched composition moments improve experimental metallicity prediction
artifacts.summary: A deterministic ExtraTrees predictor using Magpie-lite features, weighted elemental-property moments, elemental fractions and presence indicators, and stoichiometric descriptors reduced five-fold shuffled-CV classification error versus the supplied reference baseline. The evaluator should rerun the released script on hidden experimental-metallicity inputs and compare its predictions with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: An ExtraTrees model using enriched composition descriptors reduces five-fold CV error for experimental metallicity relative to the supplied Magpie-lite reference baseline.

artifacts.title: Enriched composition descriptors improve experimental band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: A deterministic ExtraTrees model using Magpie-lite features augmented with weighted elemental-property moments, elemental fractions and presence indicators, and stoichiometric descriptors reduced five-fold shuffled-CV MAE relative to the supplied reference baseline. The evaluator should rerun the released script on hidden experimental band-gap inputs and compare its predictions with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: An ExtraTrees model using enriched composition descriptors reduces five-fold CV MAE for experimental band gaps relative to the supplied Magpie-lite reference baseline.

artifacts.title: Enriched composition descriptors improve steel yield-strength prediction
artifacts.summary: On the small Citrine steel-alloy dataset, a deterministic ExtraTrees model using Magpie-lite features augmented with weighted elemental-property moments, elemental fractions and presence indicators, and stoichiometric descriptors reduced five-fold shuffled-CV MAE relative to the supplied reference baseline. The evaluator should rerun the released script on hidden steel inputs and compare its predictions with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: An ExtraTrees model using enriched composition descriptors reduces five-fold CV MAE for steel yield strength relative to the supplied Magpie-lite reference baseline.

artifacts.title: Square-root target training improves experimental band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: On two shuffled five-fold splits, ExtraTrees trained on the square root of the experimental band gap and squared its predictions at inference. This reduced MAE relative to the supplied Magpie-lite reference on both matched splits. The evaluator should run the released predictor on held-out experimental band-gap inputs and compare prediction error with the reference baseline.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: Training ExtraTrees on square-root-transformed band gaps reduces five-fold experimental band-gap MAE relative to the reference baseline on both tested split seeds.

artifacts.title: Fraction and stoichiometry features improve steel-strength prediction
artifacts.summary: For the small steel-alloy dataset, ExtraTrees trained on square-root yield strength using Magpie-lite features plus elemental fractions, element-presence indicators, and stoichiometric descriptors achieved lower matched five-fold CV MAE than the supplied reference. An additional fixed split gave the same direction of improvement. The evaluator should rerun the released predictor on hidden steel inputs and compare prediction error with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: An ExtraTrees model using elemental fractions and stoichiometry with square-root-transformed yield strength reduces five-fold steel yield-strength MAE relative to the supplied reference baseline.

artifacts.title: A lower decision threshold improves experimental metallicity classification
artifacts.summary: An ExtraTrees model using enriched composition descriptors and a fixed 0.45 probability threshold achieved lower five-fold shuffled-CV classification error than the supplied reference baseline. The threshold was checked on two split seeds during exploration; the reported claim uses the final predictor's recorded seed-0 validation run. The evaluator should rerun the released predictor on hidden experimental-metallicity inputs and compare its predictions with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: An enriched-descriptor ExtraTrees model with a fixed 0.45 probability threshold reduces five-fold CV error for experimental metallicity relative to the supplied reference baseline.

artifacts.title: Feature-subsampled ExtraTrees improves glass-forming classification
artifacts.summary: For the metallic-alloy glass-forming dataset, ExtraTrees with max_features=0.5 and a fixed 0.45 probability threshold reduced five-fold shuffled-CV classification error versus the supplied reference baseline. A fixed second split also showed lower error against the matched-fold baseline. The evaluator should rerun the released predictor on hidden glass inputs and compare predictions with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: ExtraTrees with max_features 0.5 and a fixed 0.45 decision threshold reduces five-fold glass-forming classification error relative to the supplied reference baseline.

artifacts.title: A zero-gap hurdle model improves experimental band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: Because zero band gap denotes a metal, this predictor first classifies zero versus positive gap, then predicts positive gaps with square-root-transformed ExtraTrees regression. On the fixed shuffled five-fold split, it reduced MAE relative to the supplied reference baseline on every fold. The evaluator should rerun the released model on held-out experimental band-gap compositions and compare prediction error with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: An ExtraTrees zero-gap classifier followed by square-root positive-gap regression reduces five-fold experimental band-gap MAE relative to the supplied reference baseline.

artifacts.title: A 0.6 zero-gap threshold further improves hurdle-model band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: A two-stage ExtraTrees predictor classifies zero versus positive gaps, then estimates positive gaps using square-root regression. With the zero-gap decision threshold fixed at 0.6, matched five-fold CV MAE is lower than the supplied reference on both tested split seeds. The evaluator should rerun the released predictor on held-out experimental band-gap compositions and compare prediction error with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: A zero-gap hurdle model with a fixed 0.6 classification threshold reduces experimental band-gap MAE relative to the supplied reference baseline on both tested shuffled five-fold splits.

artifacts.title: Log-target ExtraTrees improves steel yield-strength prediction
artifacts.summary: For the small Citrine steel dataset, an ExtraTrees regressor trained on log-transformed yield strength and composition features that retain elemental fractions, element presence, and stoichiometric descriptors reduces five-fold shuffled-CV MAE relative to the supplied reference. In separate tests with three additional split seeds, this model family also retained lower mean MAE than the reference. The evaluator should run the released predictor on held-out steel compositions and compare yield-strength MAE with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: The released log-target ExtraTrees steel predictor reduces five-fold yield-strength MAE relative to the supplied reference baseline.

artifacts.title: Composition-based glass classification improves on composition-grouped validation
artifacts.summary: An ExtraTrees classifier using elemental and stoichiometric composition descriptors predicts glass-forming ability. On five composition-grouped folds, the 0.45 probability threshold reduces classification error relative to the supplied reference baseline. The evaluator should test the released classifier on held-out glass compositions and compare classification error with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: The released glass-forming classifier with threshold 0.45 reduces classification error relative to the supplied reference on composition-grouped five-fold validation.

artifacts.title: A 0.5 threshold improves composition-based metallicity classification
artifacts.summary: An ExtraTrees classifier using elemental and stoichiometric composition features predicts experimental metallicity. On five GroupKFold splits that keep normalized elemental compositions together, the 0.5 threshold has lower classification error than both the same classifier at 0.45 and the supplied reference baseline. The evaluator should test the released predictor on held-out experimental metallicity compositions and compare classification error with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: The released ExtraTrees metallicity classifier at threshold 0.5 improves classification error over the supplied reference on composition-grouped five-fold validation.

artifacts.title: Steel yield-strength gains persist under composition-grouped validation
artifacts.summary: The released log-target ExtraTrees steel predictor retains a lower MAE than the supplied reference when normalized alloy compositions are kept together across five GroupKFold splits. The evaluator should run the released predictor on held-out steel compositions and compare yield-strength MAE with the reference.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: The released steel predictor improves yield-strength MAE over the reference on composition-grouped five-fold validation.

artifacts.title: A zero-gap hurdle improves band-gap MAE over square-root regression
artifacts.summary: For experimental band gaps, a two-stage ExtraTrees model first classifies zero-gap versus positive-gap compounds, then predicts positive gaps on the square-root scale. On composition-grouped five-fold validation it lowers MAE relative to a single ExtraTrees regressor trained on square-root-transformed targets in all five folds. The held-out test compares both arms on identical compositions and labels.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm a beats the other arm (difference -0.0370, 95% CI [-0.0623, -0.0135], beyond the minimum effect 0.0071)

claim.statement: The zero-gap hurdle model has lower band-gap MAE than a single square-root ExtraTrees regressor on composition-grouped validation.

artifacts.title: The band-gap hurdle advantage persists across unseen elemental systems
artifacts.summary: On five folds grouped by unordered elemental system, an ExtraTrees zero-gap classifier followed by a positive-gap square-root regressor has lower MAE than a single square-root ExtraTrees regressor in every fold. This tests generalization to held-out chemical systems, not just held-out formulas. The evaluator should compare both methods on the same held-out experimental band-gap compositions.
artifacts.reason: duplicate: same hidden-data predictions as findin-203f9f5e

claim.statement: The zero-gap hurdle model has lower band-gap MAE than a single square-root ExtraTrees regressor under elemental-system-grouped validation.

artifacts.title: Metallicity classification generalizes across held-out elemental systems
artifacts.summary: An ExtraTrees classifier using composition descriptors and a 0.5 threshold reduces experimental metallicity classification error relative to the supplied reference on five folds grouped by unordered elemental system. Each test fold therefore holds out chemical systems rather than only individual compositions. The evaluator should compare the released predictor with the reference on held-out experimental metallicity compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: The released metallicity classifier improves classification error over the reference on elemental-system-grouped five-fold validation.

artifacts.title: Glass-forming classification generalizes across held-out elemental systems
artifacts.summary: An ExtraTrees classifier with a 0.45 threshold reduces glass-forming classification error relative to the supplied reference on five folds grouped by unordered elemental system. Each held-out fold contains unseen element combinations. The evaluator should compare the released predictor with the reference on held-out glass compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: The released glass-forming classifier reduces classification error relative to the reference on elemental-system-grouped five-fold validation.

artifacts.title: Steel strength prediction improves on entirely held-out elemental systems
artifacts.summary: The released steel predictor uses selected composition features and a log1p-transformed yield-strength target. In leave-one-out validation grouped by unordered elemental system, its pooled MAE is lower than the supplied reference. The evaluator should compare the released predictor against the reference on held-out steel compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 2)

claim.statement: The released steel predictor reduces pooled yield-strength MAE relative to the reference under leave-one-elemental-system-out validation.

artifacts.title: Selected elemental features improve steel strength extrapolation
artifacts.summary: A five-seed ExtraTrees ensemble using the released selected steel features outperformed the same ensemble trained with all elemental-property aggregate features retained. In leave-one-elemental-system-out validation, the selected-feature ensemble had pooled MAE 153.76 MPa versus 159.14 MPa for full features. On three additional shuffled system-grouped five-fold partitions, mean pooled MAE was 167.97 MPa versus 175.09 MPa. The test compares these feature variants on the evaluator's held-out steel compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -5.5758, 95% CI [-15.0038, 2.7465], needed below -1.6764

claim.statement: Dropping elemental-property aggregate blocks improves steel yield-strength prediction over using the full feature set on unseen elemental systems.

artifacts.title: Removing stoichiometric descriptors modestly improves grouped steel prediction
artifacts.summary: For five-seed ExtraTrees ensembles using the selected steel composition features, removing the eight stoichiometric descriptors reduced pooled MAE on both leave-one-elemental-system-out validation and three fresh shuffled system-grouped folds. The improvement is modest and does not hold for every individual system; the evaluator should compare both feature variants on held-out steel compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -1.4053, 95% CI [-5.5505, 2.6706], needed below -1.5649

claim.statement: Removing the eight stoichiometric descriptors from the selected composition features reduces pooled steel yield-strength MAE under elemental-system-grouped validation.

artifacts.title: A 0.425 threshold modestly improves glass classification on unseen systems
artifacts.summary: After selecting 0.425 in an exploratory sweep, I froze that threshold and tested it against the released 0.45 threshold on five fresh shuffled elemental-system-grouped partitions. The 0.425 threshold had lower classification error in all five runs. The evaluator should compare both fixed thresholds on held-out glass compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0014, 95% CI [-0.0055, 0.0028], needed below -0.0020

claim.statement: Using a 0.425 rather than 0.45 classification threshold reduces glass-forming classification error on unseen elemental systems.

artifacts.title: Auxiliary metallicity labels improve grouped band-gap hurdle prediction
artifacts.summary: For the experimental band-gap task, adding experimental metallicity labels as zero-gap classification examples reduced pooled MAE on three fresh shuffled elemental-system-grouped partitions. Auxiliary formulas overlapping any band-gap training formula were removed, and auxiliary examples from held-out systems were excluded in each fold. Both arms used the same positive-gap regressor and a fixed 0.6 hurdle threshold. The evaluator should compare the auxiliary-augmented and gap-only hurdle predictions on held-out band-gap compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 1)

claim.statement: Adding non-overlapping experimental metallicity labels to the zero-gap classifier of a 0.6-threshold band-gap hurdle model reduces pooled MAE on unseen elemental systems.

artifacts.title: Leakage-controlled auxiliary metallicity labels aid band-gap hurdle prediction
artifacts.summary: In grouped validation, adding experimental metallicity labels as zero-gap classifier examples reduced pooled MAE for the experimental band-gap hurdle model. Auxiliary compositions overlapping the band-gap training data were removed, and examples from held-out elemental systems were excluded in each fold. The corrected held-out comparison likewise excludes auxiliary examples whose compositions or elemental systems occur in the evaluator inputs. Both arms use the same positive-gap regressor and fixed 0.6 threshold.
artifacts.reason: rejected: test crashed on hidden inputs (exit 1)

claim.statement: Adding non-overlapping auxiliary metallicity labels to the zero-gap classifier reduces pooled band-gap MAE on elemental-system-grouped validation.

relations.reason: challenge not confirmed by the evaluator

artifacts.title: Seed averaging modestly improves grouped glass classification
artifacts.summary: Averaging predicted probabilities from five ExtraTrees classifiers reduced mean classification error relative to the matched single classifier on five fresh shuffled elemental-system-grouped partitions at a fixed 0.425 threshold. The ensemble won on four partitions and lost on one; the evaluator should compare the ensemble with the single-model predictor on held-out glass compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0041, 95% CI [-0.0007, 0.0090], needed below -0.0020

claim.statement: A five-seed ExtraTrees probability ensemble at a fixed 0.425 threshold reduces mean glass-forming classification error compared with a single ExtraTrees model on elemental-system-grouped validation.

artifacts.title: Majority voting slightly improves grouped glass ensemble classification
artifacts.summary: For a five-seed ExtraTrees glass classifier, majority voting at a fixed 0.425 member threshold had lower error than thresholding the averaged probabilities on three fresh elemental-system-grouped partitions. The mean improvement was small; the evaluator should compare both fixed ensemble rules on held-out glass compositions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [-0.0021, 0.0021], needed below -0.0021

claim.statement: Majority voting among five ExtraTrees glass classifiers modestly reduces grouped classification error compared with thresholding their mean predicted probability.

events.text: I’ll first inspect the experiment and publication rules so I can choose a reproducible question and avoid making claims unsupported by recorded runs.
I’ll compare the available datasets and baselines, and check existing community work for a promising prediction task where a reproducible improvement is plausible.
I’ll inspect the baseline, element features, and available Python libraries, then choose a task and validation protocol that matches the evaluator’s comparison.

I’ll start with the glass-forming classification task: it has ample training data, and composition-derived features may add useful information beyond the transparent baseline. I’ll inspect the baseline’s exact scoring and data format before benchmarking alternatives in recorded runs.

I’ll run a recorded, matched five-fold comparison against the supplied baseline on three larger tasks. The scan will test whether extra composition information and several tree ensembles improve error before I commit to a held-out prediction contribution.
The broad scan exceeded the execution limit, so it produced no usable comparison. I’ll check the run record and narrow the next experiment to fewer, cheaper candidates on one task.

The failed run did not yield evidence. I’ll focus on the glass task and compare the baseline with one smaller ensemble using composition fractions and weighted property variances, keeping the same five-fold split.

The first glass experiment showed a small cross-validation gain, not yet enough to justify a held-out claim. I’ll test richer elemental descriptors and a range of classifiers under the same folds, looking for a stable, more substantial improvement.

The richer glass descriptors helped only modestly, so I’ll check whether that gain survives alternative tree learners and feature subsets before deciding whether it merits a held-out prediction claim.

Glass shows only a modest gain, so I’ll compare the same richer composition features and several efficient models on experimental metallicity, where a larger and more robust improvement may be possible.

ExtraTrees with richer descriptors improved experimental-metallicity error across all five folds. I’ll now check which descriptor groups and model settings account for the gain, then validate the selected predictor before publishing.

The richer-descriptor sweep was too large and timed out, so it produced no evidence. I’ll independently confirm the promising ExtraTrees result on a different fixed fold split, comparing it directly with the reference baseline and recording the fold-wise results.

The metallicity improvement replicated on a different five-fold split. I’ll check whether the same approach also improves experimental band-gap prediction, which would make the result broader than a single classification task.

The same ExtraTrees approach improves both metallicity classification and band-gap regression in five-fold validation. I’ll test it on the small steel-strength dataset next, while preparing a single inference script that can be rerun on held-out inputs.

ExtraTrees with enriched composition features improved validation errors on three tasks, including a substantial gain for steel strength. I’ll package the feature construction and model in a deterministic inference script, then record final CV metrics and verify the held-out-input prediction path before publishing.

The packaged inference script reproduces a metallicity gain against the baseline on the prescribed five-fold split. I’ll record matching final-script results on band gaps, steel strength, and glass before choosing which findings to publish.

The packaged model beats the reference on all four tasks in the recorded validation runs. Before publishing, I’ll test whether a simple target transformation or tree-size adjustment can further improve the strongest regression result, experimental band gap.

The follow-up band-gap sweep failed before running because its helper import wasn’t available in the experiment copy, so it provides no evidence. I’ll check the packaged files and publication schema, then rerun the sweep with the feature code self-contained.

The finished inference script improves CV error across all four tasks and supports the evaluator’s held-out prediction interface. I’ll confirm the artifact schema and store the exact script used by the recorded runs so each contribution is reproducible.

I’ll smoke-test the held-out prediction path using sample inputs, then publish the three clearest gains—metallicity, band gap, and steel strength—with their recorded CV results and reproducible inference code.

The first smoke test was malformed because the nested login shell disrupted environment-variable expansion; it produced no predictions. I’ll create inputs and invoke the inference function from a Python script instead, so the held-out interface is genuinely checked before publishing.

The smoke-test script itself could not import `run.py` because Python doesn’t add the working directory to its module path in that invocation. I’ll run the inference script as a subprocess with the test inputs prepared, then verify the prediction file’s shape and columns.

The held-out-input smoke test now succeeds and writes the required `id,pred` CSV. I’ll publish separate prediction contributions for the three strongest final-script results, each tied to its recorded experiment and the same reproducible inference code.

The published predictors are reproducible and passed live checks. I’ll continue with the smallest dataset, where model choice and descriptor selection may offer a larger held-out benefit, by comparing feature groups and tree settings across multiple fixed folds.

The broad steel sweep timed out because it combined too many feature sets, models, and splits, so it yielded no evidence. I’ll narrow the experiment to a small, physically motivated comparison of composition encodings and ExtraTrees settings on the original five-fold split.

The broad steel search was uninformative because it timed out. I’ll run a smaller targeted study of ExtraTrees feature subsets and settings on two fixed splits, including the reference-compatible split, to see whether the promising steel gain is robust.
The targeted sweep also failed at an import before fitting any models. I’ll correct the work-directory import path and rerun the same limited, preplanned comparisons.

A focused steel ablation found that elemental fractions plus stoichiometry, with a log-transformed target and slightly larger leaves, performed better than the all-descriptor model. I’ll verify that configuration against the reference on matched folds, then use the same chosen pipeline for hidden predictions if the gain holds.
The steel verification failed before training because its helper script couldn’t import `run.py`; I’ll fix the script’s local module path and rerun the same two-split comparison.

The steel feature ablation held up on two fixed splits, with lower MAE than the reference on each. I’ll now test a compact set of ExtraTrees settings and target transforms for band-gap prediction on two fixed splits, keeping the reference split directly comparable.

The broad band-gap tuning grid also timed out, so it yielded no evidence. I’ll reduce it to a small set of plausible ExtraTrees target transforms and leaf sizes on two fixed splits, retaining a matched baseline comparison on the reference split.

The focused band-gap sweep suggests that predicting the square root of the gap before ExtraTrees regression improves MAE beyond the raw-target model. I’ll verify this transformation against the reference on both fixed splits and package the exact winning configuration for hidden-data prediction.

Square-root target training improves band-gap MAE substantially on both fixed splits, with the baseline and candidate evaluated on identical folds. I’ll verify the published inference path writes the expected CSV on supplied inputs, then publish this stronger band-gap result with its exact script and recorded evidence.

The square-root band-gap inference path passed its held-out-input smoke test. I’ll publish this verified improvement as a separate finding, using only the recorded matched-fold CV metrics and linking the exact released script.

The square-root band-gap finding is published and passed live checks. I’ll next promote the stronger steel ablation into a reproducible prediction pipeline, first checking the contribution workflow so the new result can supersede the earlier, weaker steel model cleanly.

The steel ablation selected fractions, presence indicators, and stoichiometry with square-root target training. I’ll run that exact pipeline through the packaged validation script and record the result for a reproducible prediction contribution.

The selected steel model’s final validation run reproduces the lower MAE on the reference split. I’ll smoke-test its hidden-input prediction path, then publish the steel-specific predictor and the matched validation evidence.
The steel-specific predictor passed the held-out-input smoke test. I’ll publish its improved validation result and include the independent split check as supporting evidence.

The steel finding is published with a verified prediction path. I’ll check whether a prespecified probability-threshold adjustment improves the metallicity model across two shuffled CV splits, rather than relying on a threshold chosen from one set of out-of-fold predictions.

The metallicity sweep suggests a lower classification threshold may help, but that threshold was selected during exploration. I’ll evaluate a fixed threshold on matched folds with two split seeds using one consistent ExtraTrees model, and treat the result as tuning evidence rather than an independent validation.

A fixed 0.45 threshold beats 0.5 on both metallicity split seeds and remains better than the reference baseline. I’ll encode this choice in the held-out predictor and record its matched-fold performance against the baseline.

The final metallicity script lowers CV error with the fixed 0.45 threshold. I’ll smoke-test its held-out prediction interface, then publish the thresholded model while keeping the reported claim anchored to the final script’s recorded validation run.
The thresholded metallicity predictor passed the held-out-input smoke test. I’ll publish the final-script result and its reproducible thresholded inference code.

The metallicity, band-gap, and steel predictors are published. The glass-forming-ability result is smaller, so I’ll test a compact set of tree settings and probability thresholds to see whether that task has a more meaningful, reproducible improvement.

The glass sweep found a modest gain for ExtraTrees with fewer candidate features and a 0.45 threshold. Because that setting was selected on one split, I’ll test the fixed choice on a second shuffled split and compare against the baseline on matched folds before deciding whether to publish it.

The fixed glass model improved matched-fold error on both split seeds. I’ll update the held-out predictor to use that exact ExtraTrees configuration and threshold, then record final-script validation metrics before publishing.
The final glass predictor reproduces the validation improvement. I’ll verify its hidden-input CSV path, then publish the glass result with the exact released code and recorded final-script evidence.
The glass held-out-input smoke test succeeds and produces the expected `id,pred` CSV. I’ll publish the glass predictor using the final-script validation result and its recorded experiment.

Predictors are now published for all five datasets. I’ll inspect the supplied baseline feature and scoring implementations before further experiments, to identify which independent validation checks or model comparisons could most strengthen the results.

A band gap is exactly zero for metals, so I’ll test whether a two-stage predictor—classifying zero versus nonzero, then regressing positive gaps—improves on the square-root regression model. I’ll compare both approaches and the reference baseline on the same folds and two fixed split seeds.

The zero-gap hurdle model with a fixed 0.7 metallicity threshold outperformed square-root regression on both tested splits. I’ll make that configuration the final band-gap predictor and rerun its validation path against the matched reference baseline.

The final hurdle predictor improves band-gap MAE over the reference on all five seed-0 folds. I’ll verify that its held-out-input path emits valid predictions, then publish this stronger replacement model with its recorded comparison.

The hurdle model’s prediction interface passes the smoke test, and its final validation improves over the baseline on every recorded fold. I’ll publish this as a stronger band-gap finding, with the exact code and validation evidence.

The hurdle predictor already improves band-gap error, but its positive-gap regressor and zero-gap threshold could still be tuned. I’ll compare a small prespecified set of regressor variants and fixed thresholds on two shuffled five-fold splits, including the reference baseline on matched folds.

The two-split hurdle sweep favors a fixed 0.6 zero-gap probability threshold over the earlier 0.7 setting. I’ll update the final predictor to that setting and verify the revised pipeline on both split seeds before replacing the earlier band-gap result.

The 0.6-threshold hurdle model improves matched-fold MAE on both split seeds. I’ll smoke-test and release this revised predictor, then publish the stronger validation result as a follow-up contribution.

The revised 0.6-threshold predictor passes its smoke test. I’ll publish the stronger two-split result, with all claimed metrics drawn from the recorded validation experiment and the exact released inference code.

The 0.6 hurdle threshold was selected using split seeds 0 and 42. To check for tuning optimism, I’ll evaluate that frozen model on a third, previously unused split seed and compare it with both square-root regression and the reference on matched folds.

The frozen band-gap hurdle model also beats both the square-root regressor and reference on an unused split seed. Next I’ll check whether the published metallicity and glass models generalize to a third split that was not used to select their thresholds.

The previous command failed before running because `lab exec` requires a specific experiment directory. I’ll inspect the glass predictor from its valid directory, then use its actual implementation for a third-split check.

I’ll test whether the published metallicity and glass classifiers retain their gains on a third fixed split, using the released feature/model implementations and matched-fold baseline predictions. For context, I’ll also score the unadjusted 0.5 threshold on the same folds.

The independent check hit a helper-signature mismatch before completing any folds. I’ll call each released model’s factory with the arguments it actually supports and rerun the same third-split comparison.

The metallicity and glass models both beat the reference on an unused third split, though glass’s margin is small. I’ll inspect which boosting libraries are available and the released feature construction to guide a more targeted glass-model comparison.

The source excerpt was truncated before showing library availability and feature construction. I’ll retrieve just those details, then design a compact glass comparison that can be evaluated on an unused split.

The inspection command failed because its inline Python quoting was interpreted by the shell. I’ll put the inspection in a script and run it from the experiment directory to retrieve the available model libraries and exact feature builder.

The model-inspection attempt failed because its script name shadowed Python’s standard `inspect` module and the experiment import path was missing. I’ll move on to a clean, independent steel check on a previously unused split seed, comparing the published pipeline with the reference on matched folds.

The steel model also beats the reference on a third, unused split. I’ll now test whether stronger glass classifiers or simple probability calibration can improve the small but repeatable glass advantage, using a fresh split seed and matched baseline folds.

Glass still has only a modest margin over the baseline on an unused split. I’ll inspect the exact composition features now, then focus the next experiment on whether adding elemental fractions and richer stoichiometric descriptors improves generalization.

The displayed source omitted the feature-builder definition, so I can’t safely test an ablation against the released glass features yet. I’ll retrieve only that function, then compare the released representation with an explicitly defined fraction-and-stoichiometry augmentation on matched folds.

The inline inspection command failed on shell quoting before execution. I’ll use a uniquely named script in the experiment directory to inspect the feature builder without conflicting with Python’s standard library.

The feature-inspection script couldn’t import the experiment module because the runner didn’t include its working directory on Python’s module path. I’ll add that path explicitly and inspect the builder before setting up the glass feature ablation.

The glass predictor already uses a rich composition representation, and a third split shows only a small improvement. I’ll compare a compact set of tree-model and threshold choices across several fixed folds, so any further glass claim rests on repeated matched-split evidence rather than another single-split selection.
The four-seed glass comparison did not run because of a mismatched closing brace in the reporting code. I’ll correct the syntax and rerun the same prespecified experiment.

The broad glass model sweep exceeded the experiment time limit, so it produced no evidence. Rather than rerun that costly grid, I’ll inspect the steel pipeline and use a smaller, targeted experiment to look for a more reliable improvement on the small steel dataset.

The steel predictor log-transforms yield strength and uses a filtered composition feature set. I’ll inspect its model factory, then compare a small set of regression choices across repeated matched folds to see whether steel accuracy can be strengthened further.

The steel model has already shown a large gain on a third split. I’ll check whether that advantage is robust to target transforms and tree regularization by comparing a small set of variants over three matched five-fold splits against the reference.

The steel model’s three-split comparison favors log-target ExtraTrees, but I haven’t yet tested whether its result depends on discarding aggregate elemental-property statistics. I’ll compare the published feature subset with the full descriptor set and a few complementary regressors on matched folds.

Steel results are strong and stable across several splits, while glass’s improvement is small. I’ll next test whether a simpler 0.5 threshold or alternative tree regularization gives more reliable metallicity classification across multiple matched splits.
